85.title: The butter thief
85.hook: a toddler with butter on his chin, a line of happy monkeys, and the neighbors at his mother's door
85.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small image of baby Krishna, often called Laddu Gopal, and bathe, dress and offer food to him each day; the butter-thief stories are told and sung, especially around Janmashtami.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rakhi, a thread on a wrist and a promise of protection. Today, the man who held Arjuna's reins, back when he was small enough to steal butter.

A village of cowherds on the banks of the Yamuna, early morning. The women have been churning since before dawn, and the fresh butter is hung high in clay pots, out of reach. It doesn't help. By noon a pot is cracked, the butter is gone, and a line of monkeys is licking their fingers. The culprit is about three years old. He has butter on his chin, and he swears he was asleep. The women march to his mother's door to complain, and halfway through complaining, they start laughing.
screen: `BUTTER, HUNG OUT OF REACH.` → `A LINE OF HAPPY MONKEYS.` → `HE SWEARS HE WAS ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, the same Krishna you left holding Arjuna's reins on day seventy-seven. The Bhagavata Purana gives the neighbors' complaint as a list. He lets the calves loose before milking time. He steals the curd and the butter. He feeds it to the monkeys, and if the monkeys won't eat, he breaks the pot. When the pots are hung out of reach, he stacks up stools and a mortar and climbs. And when he's caught, he looks so innocent that nobody can stay angry. That's why the nickname stuck. In Hindi he's Makhan Chor, the butter thief, and it's always said with love. This same Krishna is honored as God. In the Gita he speaks as the source of everything, and in the same life he's a toddler being scolded by his mother. Devotees don't treat that as a contradiction. Many say it's the point: God close enough to be fed, chased, scolded and loved like a child. So Krishna comes with many faces. The baby born in a prison at midnight. The butter thief. The cowherd boy whose flute pulls the whole village outside. The friend driving a chariot onto a battlefield. Many people love one face most. In many homes there's a small brass baby Krishna, crawling, a sweet in one hand, often called Laddu Gopal. Families bathe him, dress him and offer him food each day, the way you'd care for a little child. Gopala means a cowherd, the one who looks after the cows. And the butter? Some devotees say it stands for a soft, well-churned heart, and that a heart is what he really comes to steal.
screen: `A THIEF THE WHOLE VILLAGE LOVES.` · `THE SAME KRISHNA, HONORED AS GOD.` · `ONE PERSON, MANY FACES.` · `THE BABY ON THE HOME SHRINE.`

segments.voice: Picture someone small you love caught mid-mischief, a child, a sibling, a pet: wide eyes, guilty grin, evidence on the chin. Notice the annoyance, maybe, and right under it something softer, and stay with the softer thing. If you pray, you can hold Krishna's child face in your mind the same way.
Makhan Chor. The butter thief: Krishna as a little boy, scolded and adored, and still honored as God. Today's word.
Your line: close enough to scold. A God you can chase around the kitchen. Day eighty-five, and the butter's gone.

86.title: Banana peels for Krishna
86.hook: Krishna turns down a palace feast and eats at a humble house, where he's handed the peels
86.carry: bhava: god takes the feeling, not the finish
86.howItsDone: Many families bring home or make a clay Ganesha for Ganesh Chaturthi, often of natural clay so it dissolves at the immersion; in many pujas Ganesha is first invoked in a small cone of turmeric paste or a betel nut. Devotional songs retell Krishna eating at Vidura's house.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the butter thief, honored as God. Close enough to scold. Today, Krishna grown up, turning down the best dinner in the city.

Remember day seventy-five: Krishna in Hastinapura, asking for peace. Duryodhana has laid out a feast to win him over, gold plates, every dish the palace kitchens can make. Krishna says no. In the Mahabharata he puts it plainly: people eat at someone's table out of love, or out of need, and here there's neither. Then he walks across the city to the small house of Vidura, the old king's wise, humble half-brother. Nobody there is expecting God for dinner.
screen: `A FEAST TO WIN KRISHNA OVER.` → `NOT LOVE, NOT NEED: REFUSED.` → `TO VIDURA'S SMALL HOUSE INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Families love to tell what happened next, in a telling sung in devotional songs more than written in the epic. Vidura's wife is home when Krishna walks in, and she's so overjoyed she can't think straight. She sits him down, grabs some bananas, peels them, and in her excitement throws the fruit aside and hands him the peels. And Krishna eats them, one after another, smiling, as if he's never tasted anything better. When Vidura gets home he's horrified, and serves the fruit properly. Krishna takes a bite and says, gently, it isn't as sweet as the peels. That's the teaching, and it has a name: bhava, the feeling inside an offering. An old Sanskrit saying makes the same point with a grammar joke: one person says Vishnu's name with the ending wrong, a scholar says it right, and both earn the same, because God takes the feeling. It's why Hindus worship the way they do. Today's word, murti, is a form God is invited into. A temple murti may be carved by trained hands, but in many pujas Ganesha is first called into a little cone of turmeric paste, or a single betel nut. No trunk, no ears. Shiva is honored as a smooth stone. Now, a kitchen table, the week before Ganesh Chaturthi. Someone has made a clay Ganesha for the family shrine. The trunk leans; one ear is bigger. Next to the perfect ones online it looks clumsy, and the worry comes: am I doing this wrong? Krishna ate the peels. The feeling is the offering; the clay carries it.
screen: `VIDURA'S WIFE HANDS HIM PEELS.` · `NOT AS SWEET AS THE PEELS.` · `BHAVA: THE FEELING INSIDE THE OFFERING.` · `MURTI: A FORM GOD IS INVITED INTO.` · then, large: `GOD TAKES THE FEELING, NOT THE FINISH.`

segments.voice: This is the oldest offering there is. Pick one small thing you can give: a flower, a piece of fruit, a spoon of something you cooked, or just a glass of water. Notice the voice that says it isn't enough, not fancy, not done right; let it talk. Then picture Vidura's wife, so happy she handed God the peels, and Krishna smiling as he ate. If you have a shrine or a picture of God at home, set your offering before it with both hands, the way families offer food before a meal, and say a name you love, Krishna or Ganesha, once. If you don't pray, set it down for someone you love, a parent or a friend, and give it with your whole heart. Either way, the gift is the feeling. Stay with that for a few breaths.
Murti. A form, a body: the shape God is invited into, from carved stone to a cone of turmeric, honored for the love inside it. Today's word.
Your line: bhava, God takes the feeling, not the finish. Krishna ate the peels. On to day eighty-seven.

87.title: Who else is there?
87.hook: a demon king proposes to the Goddess; she answers with a vow, and shows that every goddess is her
87.howItsDone: During Navaratri, Hindus honor the Goddess for nine nights with fasting, prayers and songs; in Gujarat people dance garba and dandiya, in Bengal Durga Puja is celebrated, and in the south homes display rows of dolls. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, celebrates victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the murti, and Krishna eating the peels at Vidura's house. Bhava, God takes the feeling. Today, the Goddess, and the rest of her story.

The buffalo demon is dead. You may know that story already: the gods' light pouring together into the Goddess, the lion, the shape-changing fight, her spear and sword at the end. On the nights of Navaratri, the text that tells it, the Devi Mahatmya, is read aloud in homes and temples. And the text doesn't stop at the buffalo. A few chapters later, two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken heaven. Their servants bring word of a beautiful woman alone in the Himalayas. And the brothers make a very bad decision. They send her a marriage proposal.
screen: `THE TEXT DOESN'T STOP AT THE BUFFALO.` → `TWO DEMON BROTHERS.` → `A MARRIAGE PROPOSAL.`

segments.voice: Shumbha's messenger arrives with the offer. The king of the three worlds wants you, he says; all the treasures of heaven are his, and they could be yours. The Goddess answers politely. What you say is true, she tells him. But long ago I made a vow, a foolish one: whoever defeats me in battle, whoever breaks my pride, whoever is my equal in strength, he will be my husband. So tell your king to come and win me. He goes back, and the brothers send an army. When the generals Chanda and Munda come for her, her face darkens with anger, and from her forehead springs Kali, gaunt and terrible, who destroys them both. So the Goddess gives Kali a name: Chamunda, the one who ended Chanda and Munda. One by one the army falls. Nishumbha falls. At the end Shumbha, the last, shouts at her: you're proud, but you only win because others fight for you. She answers: I am alone in the world here. Who else is there besides me? All the goddesses who fought beside her flow back into her body, and she faces him as one. Then she wins. That's the teaching under the whole festival. Hindus honor many goddesses: fierce Kali, generous Lakshmi, Saraswati with her veena. In this text, they're all one Goddess, Devi, the Mother, showing different faces. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Through these nights the text is read, many families honor a different form of her each night, and they still call her by one name: Ma. One Goddess, many forms.
screen: `A PROPOSAL, AND A VOW.` · `KALI SPRINGS FROM HER FOREHEAD.` · `WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?` · `NAVA, NINE. RATRI, NIGHT.` · then, large: `ONE GODDESS, MANY FORMS.`

segments.voice: Through Navaratri many Hindus light a small lamp before the Goddess each night and call her Ma. If you pray, light one, or picture one, and say a few of her names slowly: Durga, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kali. Notice how different they feel, fierce, generous, wise, wild, and hold them as one face. If you don't pray, think of someone you know who is many things at once, and still one person.
Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights of the Goddess, and a tenth day of victory.
Your line: one goddess, many forms. Who else is there besides me? Every name is hers. Until tomorrow.

88.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
88.hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
88.carry: the guest is god: light the way
88.howItsDone: At Diwali, Hindus clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps on the new-moon night of Kartika, worship Lakshmi, open new account books, share sweets and visit family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri: the Goddess who drew every goddess back into herself. One goddess, many forms. Today, the darkest night of the month, and a row of little lamps.

You've heard Diwali's great story: Rama coming home to Ayodhya after fourteen years in the forest, and a city lighting lamps to show him the way. Tonight, look at the lamps themselves. It's the new-moon night of the month of Kartika, in autumn. No moon at all. On every windowsill, every doorstep, every railing, there's a small clay dish of oil with a cotton wick. Dozens of them. Hundreds, on a single street. Somebody's grandmother has been on her knees since the afternoon, drawing a pattern in colored powder at the front door. The door is wide open. Somebody is expected.
screen: `THE NEW-MOON NIGHT.` → `A LAMP ON EVERY SILL.` → `THE DOOR IS WIDE OPEN.`

segments.voice: Diwali is the everyday form of the Sanskrit Deepavali. Deepa is a lamp. Avali is a row. A row of lamps: the whole festival in two words. Not one big light, but a row of small ones, each a clay dish you could hold in your palm. And they come on the darkest night on purpose, the new moon of Kartika. If you wanted to show light winning, you'd pick exactly this night. So who is expected? Rama, in the Ramayana's story. And in many homes, on the main night, Lakshmi too, the Goddess of wealth and good fortune. Families clean the house from top to bottom in the days before, because the tradition says she comes to homes that are clean, bright and open. They draw rangoli, those patterns of colored powder, at the threshold. They leave doors and windows open and lamps burning so she can find the house. The whole night is an act of welcome: a clean house, a lit path, an open door. Hindus grow up with an old Sanskrit line for this: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be God to you. On Diwali it runs both ways. God is welcomed like a guest, and every guest who walks in is welcomed like God. And look at who the lamps are for. You can see your own house without them. They're for someone coming in out of the dark. The guest is God.
screen: `DEEPA, A LAMP. AVALI, A ROW.` · `THE DARKEST NIGHT, ON PURPOSE.` · `A CLEAN HOUSE, AN OPEN DOOR.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA.` · then, large: `THE GUEST IS GOD.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle, or switch on one small lamp and turn the others off; if you can't, picture a clay lamp on your windowsill, and watch the flame. Think of the people who come home to you, or the ones you come home to: a partner on a late shift, a kid walking back from school, a parent you visit on Sundays. Picture your small light at the door, already lit, when they arrive.
Diwali. From Deepavali, a row of lamps, lit on the darkest night of Kartika for someone coming home.
Your line: the guest is God, so light the way. Somebody is expected, and the door is open. That's day eighty-eight.

89.title: Why is Krishna blue?
89.hook: the texts call Krishna, Rama and Draupadi dark; so why is he blue on the calendar and fair on the screen?
89.howItsDone: Devotional songs call Krishna Shyam or Ghanashyam, dark as a rain cloud; temple images show him dark, often black stone, and paintings usually show him blue; in Braj, Holi is played in his and Radha's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali: a row of lamps on the darkest night, and an open door. The guest is God. Today, a question kids ask about the boy on the calendar.

Look at the calendar on almost any Hindu kitchen wall. Krishna is blue. Not a little blue: sky blue, peacock blue, swimming-pool blue. Now look at many of the films and TV shows made about him. Often he's played by a fair-skinned actor with a gym body. Then open the old texts. They agree with neither picture. So which one is he? Today, the color of the gods.
screen: `BLUE ON THE CALENDAR.` → `FAIR ON THE SCREEN.` → `WHAT DO THE TEXTS SAY?`

segments.voice: Start with his name. In Sanskrit, krishna means dark, even black. Some teachers also hear in it the one who draws you in, from a root that means to pull, and plenty of devotees happily keep both. But the color is right there in the name. The devotional poems call him Ghanashyam: dark as a rain cloud, the heavy blue-black cloud just before the monsoon breaks. In songs he's simply Shyam, the dark one. And he isn't alone. In the Ramayana, Rama too is described as dark. In the Mahabharata, Draupadi is called Krishnaa, the dark one, for her complexion, and Arjuna says one of his own names, Krishna, came from his dark skin. Dark, and in every case, beautiful. The one Hindus love as God was pictured dark, and loved for exactly that. So where did the blue come from? Painters reached for the deep blue of a rain cloud, and over the centuries it brightened. Many devotees add a meaning: blue is the color of the sky and the ocean, the things with no edge. And the fair actors? Posters and films have often cast that way. The texts never asked for it. Many Hindus talk about this openly now, and nobody needs to blame one artist to see the gap. Braj even has a Holi story about it. 90.title: The pillar with no end
90.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
90.carry: no top, no bottom: shiva is endless
90.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a night-long vigil in Shiva temples, pour water, milk and bilva leaves over the lingam, and chant Om Namah Shivaya; many temple carvings show Shiva appearing from the pillar of light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shyama: Krishna, dark as a rain cloud, and praised for it. Today, Shiva's night again, and a pillar with no end.

Two gods are arguing. Brahma, the creator, says: I made everything, so I'm the greatest. Vishnu, the preserver, says: I hold everything together, so I am. It's an argument you could hear at any dinner table: who matters most. And it's getting heated. Then, between them, out of nowhere, a column of fire bursts up out of the ground. It rises past the clouds and goes down past anything they can see. No top, no bottom. Both of them stop talking.
screen: `WHO IS THE GREATEST?` → `A COLUMN OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: This story is told in the Shiva Purana, and in others too. The two gods make a deal: whoever finds the end of the pillar wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and digs down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go for what the story calls ages. Vishnu never reaches the bottom. He comes back and says, honestly: I couldn't find it. Brahma never reaches the top. On the way he sees a flower drifting down, and in many tellings he takes it back as proof and claims he found the top. He didn't. Then the pillar opens, and Shiva steps out of it. The light was him all along. In the tellings, Vishnu is honored for his honesty, and Brahma is rebuked for the lie. This is one of the stories people tell about the lingam, the rounded stone at the heart of a Shiva temple. Some understand it as a small image of that pillar of light: no beginning, no end. Some say this is the night it happened, the great night of Shiva. Now the teaching. The argument was about who was biggest. The answer was something neither god could measure. For Shiva's devotees, he isn't one more god in the lineup; he's the endless reality the gods themselves come from. That's why the lingam has no face: a form for the one beyond form. And the two gods? Brahma's pride wanted to say, I reached the end. Vishnu's honest I couldn't was the right answer to the infinite. No top, no bottom.
screen: `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `NEITHER FINDS THE END.` · `THE PILLAR OPENS: SHIVA.` · `THE LINGAM: A FORM FOR THE FORMLESS.` · then, large: `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: On this night many Hindus pour water over the lingam and repeat Om Namah Shivaya, I bow to Shiva. If you pray, say it softly eleven times, or pour a glass of water slowly as an offering. If you don't, picture the pillar of light, rising and sinking farther than you can follow. When the voice comes that says that's enough, take three more breaths.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva. For many, the night the pillar of light appeared, with no top and no bottom.
Your line: no top, no bottom: Shiva is endless. Neither god could measure him. See you tomorrow.

91.title: Indrani's thread
91.hook: a queen ties a blessed thread on the king of the gods before battle; centuries later, strangers tie them in the street
91.carry: anyone can tie the thread of protection
91.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
91.howItsDone: On Raksha Bandhan sisters tie rakhis on brothers, and in many regions family priests tie protective threads on the people they serve; the thread is also tied between friends, cousins and neighbors as a sign of care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shivaratri: a pillar of light with no top and no bottom. Shiva is endless. Today, the thread again, and where it came from.

Some of the stories about the protective thread aren't about a brother and a sister at all. There's a king of the gods, going out to a war he's losing, and his wife, who won't let him go empty-handed. And much later, there's a province about to be split in two, where people walk into the street and tie threads on strangers. The rakhi glittering on cardboard in shop windows each summer has a longer, stranger history than the sibling ritual alone.
screen: `NOT ALWAYS A BROTHER AND SISTER.` → `A KING OF THE GODS AT WAR.` → `A PROVINCE ABOUT TO SPLIT.`

segments.voice: First, the king. A story told in the Bhavishya Purana, and repeated at many rakhi ceremonies, says that Indra, king of the gods, was being beaten by the demons. His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, prepared a protective thread, blessed with sacred words, and tied it on his wrist on the full moon of Shravana. He went back into battle and won. So here the thread is tied by a wife on a husband, before a fight. Second, the priests. In many parts of India, on this same full moon, a family priest ties a protective thread on the wrists of the people he serves. The thread was never only one relationship. It's a blessing you can put on anyone you want to keep safe. Third, closer to our time. In 1905, the British government divided the province of Bengal. On the day the division took effect, the poet Rabindranath Tagore called on people to tie rakhis on one another, Hindus and Muslims alike, as a sign that the people of Bengal would not be split. People walked through Calcutta tying threads on neighbors and strangers. A wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister. That's the teaching inside the thread: raksha, protection, is a sacred promise tied with a prayer, and no one relationship owns it. Anyone you'd keep safe can wear it. And that's the week. A butter thief, banana peels at Vidura's house, one Goddess in many forms, lamps for a divine guest, a boy dark as a rain cloud, a pillar with no end, and a thread.
screen: `INDRANI TIES IT ON INDRA.` · `A PRIEST TIES IT ON HIS PEOPLE.` · `1905: THREADS ON STRANGERS.` · `RAKSHA: A PROMISE OF PROTECTION.` · then, large: `ANYONE CAN TIE THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Let a first face come, someone you'd protect, maybe the one from last time; then a second, someone who isn't family: a coworker going through something, a neighbor who lives alone, someone you disagree with. Picture tying a thread on their wrist too, and say inside: I'd look out for you. Stay with both faces for a few breaths.
Rakhi. The thread of protection, tied by a wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister. Always holding a promise.
